Breaks with rolling are much easier to fix, as you can roll back a package or a set of packages which caused an issue until a fix is available.

Fixed releases have no such luck, as if you have issues with Mint 18 after upgrading from 17.3, what can you do?

Nothing so far as I am aware, except format and reinstall 17.3.

It's quite possible to roll back packages on fixed release distros. It's also much less likely to have a broken package at all on a fixed release distro. That's the idea of them after all. Sure you have to wait longer for the backported packages when they have updates.

Also I would never advise someone to "upgrade" from release to release on a fixed release distro, upgrades instead of fresh installs are what causes the most problems. If you want something like that you need a separate home folder or to just run a rolling release that isn't bleeding edge like PCLinuxOS.

Yeah, I wasn't very accurate in my comment.

I suppose it would be more accurate to say it is harder to fix issues on a fixed release after an upgrade, rather than impossible.

Fixed releases like to portray themselves as more stable, but in reality they just defer the headache you are going to get with updating. Rolling keeps throwing updates at you, in much smaller chunks, which makes it easier to identify what update caused your issue, since you only have a short list of potential suspects to wade through.

Fixed distros save it all up and then throw it at you all at once.

If something breaks, you are left with a mile long list of packages that were updated, having to wade through which combination of them are at fault. And God help you if you have multiple issues.

The thing is, they know the way they do things is inefficient and broken, which is why you get projects like Mint saying: better to do a fresh install mate. We don't officially recommend upgrading.

Fixed release are more stable on a fresh install, there's no question of that. Like I said thats the whole idea. Things just aren't likely to break at all. The trade off is that you get is you get old packages for longer periods. Yes, something like Ubuntu LTS will give you knew software versions but you will have to wait 6 months between for the point releases ie: 16.04.1, 16.04.2 where on Manjaro you only have to wait a few weeks while the Manjaro devs test them (or wait for Arch users to smooth out the edges for them).

Upgrading fixed release distros is where the problems come in, in my experience. There were a lot of problems especially when debian/canonical switched to systemd and people were still given the advice from media outlets to upgrade fixed release distros and tons of people ended up with problems, me included.

You are right about the troubleshooting being a lot easier on rolling releases than upgrades of fixed releases.
